nameStory: Great burnet gets its name from its impressive size compared to its smaller cousin, salad burnet. The word 'burnet' comes from the French 'brunette,' referring to the dark reddish-brown color of the flower heads. Medieval herbalists called it 'Sanguisorba,' meaning 'blood-absorber,' because they believed it could heal wounds and stop bleeding.
description: Great burnet is a tall, stately wildflower that can reach 3-6 feet in height, making it one of the more imposing members of the rose family. It produces distinctive oval-shaped flower heads that look like dark red thimbles perched atop long, sturdy stems. The compound leaves are made up of many small, toothed leaflets that give the plant a feathery appearance. Despite being in the rose family, it looks nothing like a typical rose and is more reminiscent of a prairie wildflower.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, oval flower heads about 1-2 inches long that look like dark red or burgundy thimbles. The tiny individual flowers lack petals but have prominent red stamens that give the heads their rich color and slightly fuzzy texture.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-15 oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem, each leaflet with rounded teeth along the edges. When crushed, the leaves smell faintly cucumber-like and feel smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright perennial that forms clumps, with flower stems rising well above the foliage. The stems are smooth, sturdy, and often have a reddish tinge that matches the flower color.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry fruits develop within the flower heads after blooming, turning the once-colorful heads into brown, papery structures that persist into fall.

habitat: Great burnet thrives in moist meadows, wet prairies, and the edges of marshes or streams throughout New England. It prefers rich, consistently moist soils and full sun to partial shade, often growing alongside other wetland wildflowers like joe-pye weed and swamp milkweed. You might also find it in roadside ditches or low-lying areas where water collects.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as clusters of compound leaves close to the ground, with the characteristic toothed leaflets unfurling in a fresh green color.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer, when the distinctive dark red flower heads appear on tall stems above the foliage, creating an impressive display.
seasonality.fall: Flower heads turn brown and papery but remain on the stems, while leaves may take on yellowish tones before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground completely, leaving no above-ground traces except occasionally some persistent dried flower heads on old stems.

funFact: Great burnet is like a butterfly nursery for some of Europe's rarest butterflies - the large blue butterflies actually lay their eggs exclusively on burnet plants, and their caterpillars depend entirely on this one plant species to survive, making great burnet a critical conservation species across the Atlantic.
confusionNotes: Great burnet's thimble-like flower heads might be confused with red clover from a distance, but clover has the typical three-part leaves and rounder, pinker flower heads. Remember: burnet has 'burnt' colored heads and compound leaves with many leaflets, while clover has three leaflets and lighter-colored, fluffier flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, great burnet shares few obvious characteristics with roses, lacking both thorns and showy petals. This demonstrates how diverse plant families can be - the rose family includes everything from apples and strawberries to this prairie-like wildflower, all united by subtle flower structure similarities.
compareHints: Great burnet towers over its relatives, reaching 3-6 feet compared to Canadian burnet's 2-4 feet and salad burnet's modest 1-2 feet. While Canadian burnet has white bottlebrush-like flowers and salad burnet has small greenish heads, great burnet's dark red thimble-shaped flowers are unmistakable. Great burnet also prefers wetter habitats than its drier-loving cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian burnet is the tallest burnet species you'll find in New England, easily distinguished from its relatives by its creamy white flowers (great burnet has dark red flowers, while salad burnet has tiny greenish flowers with red tips).
Unlike its relatives Canadian burnet and great burnet which are native and have white or pink flowers, salad burnet has those distinctive dark crimson flower heads and is much smaller overall.
Siberian Burnet is the only burnet in New England with drooping flower spikes - all other burnets have upright flower heads.
